lessons.title: Essential Calculation Formulas for Nurses
lessons.lay_summary: Nurses use four core formulas to calculate drug doses safely. Practice these until they become automatic — they are tested on NCLEX and used every shift.

content.intro: Medication calculation errors are a leading cause of patient harm. Competence in dose calculation is a fundamental nursing skill, not optional.

sections.title: The Basic Dose Formula
sections.body:
Dose ordered ÷ Dose on hand × Vehicle = Volume to administer.
Example: Order: amoxicillin 375 mg. Available: 250 mg/5 mL suspension.
375 ÷ 250 × 5 mL = 7.5 mL
Always label your units. The vehicle (mL, tablet) must match what you have.

sections.title: Weight-Based Dosing (mg/kg)
sections.body:
1. Calculate total dose: weight (kg) × dose (mg/kg) = total dose (mg).
2. Convert to volume: total dose ÷ concentration (mg/mL) = mL to administer.
Example: Patient 70 kg, order gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV. Stock: 40 mg/mL.
Step 1: 70 × 5 = 350 mg.
Step 2: 350 ÷ 40 = 8.75 mL.
Always verify that the calculated dose is within the safe therapeutic range.

sections.title: Infusion Rate: mL/h
sections.body:
mL/h = Total volume (mL) ÷ Time (hours).
Example: 1000 mL NS over 8 hours → 1000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/h.
For IV pumps this is all you need to set. Programme the pump — never estimate gravity drip rate without calculating drops/min.

sections.title: Drip Rate: Drops per Minute (Gravity Infusion)
sections.body:
Drops/min = (Volume mL × Drop factor) ÷ (Time in hours × 60 min).
Drop factors: macrodrip 10 or 15 gtt/mL (blood, viscous fluids); 20 gtt/mL (standard); microdrip 60 gtt/mL (paediatrics, critical drugs).
Example: 500 mL over 6 h, drop factor 20 gtt/mL:
(500 × 20) ÷ (6 × 60) = 10 000 ÷ 360 = 27.8 → round to 28 gtt/min.
Count drops for 15 seconds × 4 to confirm at the bedside.

sections.title: Unit Conversion Reference
sections.body:
Weight: 1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 mcg (μg); 1 kg = 2.2 lb.
Volume: 1 L = 1000 mL.
Time: 1 h = 60 min.
Common error: mcg/kg/min infusions — ensure all units are consistent before calculating pump rate.

content.clinical_pearl: Dimensional analysis (factor-label method) is the safest approach: arrange units so they cancel until only the answer unit remains. Example: 5 mg/kg × 70 kg × (1 mL/40 mg) = 8.75 mL. Units cancel cleanly → if they don't cancel, the formula is wrong.
key_points: Basic formula: Ordered ÷ On hand × Vehicle = Volume
Weight-based: kg × mg/kg = mg total, then mg ÷ concentration = mL
Infusion rate: Total mL ÷ hours = mL/h
Always include units in your calculation to catch errors
references: Ogden SJ. Calculation of Drug Dosages, 2014

lessons.title: IV Therapy: Access, Compatibility, and Complications
lessons.lay_summary: IV lines provide direct access to the bloodstream — the fastest but most dangerous route. Nurses must know how to choose and maintain IV access and recognise complications early.

content.intro: Intravenous therapy is the most direct drug delivery route. Speed of onset means errors act quickly. Nursing responsibilities include insertion (peripheral), maintenance, monitoring, and complication recognition.

sections.title: Peripheral IV Access
sections.body: Choose the smallest gauge catheter that delivers the required therapy. Larger gauge = faster flow rate but more vein trauma. 18 G for blood/trauma; 20–22 G routine medications; 24 G paediatrics/fragile veins. Preferred sites: forearm veins (cephalic, basilic, median cubital). Avoid: dominant hand if possible, wrist, antecubital (mobility limits), lower extremities (thrombosis risk). Change peripheral IVs per policy (72–96 h or clinical indication).

sections.title: Drug Compatibility
sections.body: Never assume drugs are compatible. Precipitate formation can cause emboli. Key incompatibility examples: phenytoin + dextrose (precipitates); furosemide + gentamicin (same line without flush); TPN + medications (most incompatible). Resources: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs, Micromedex. When in doubt: flush with 0.9% NaCl before and after each drug; use separate lumens on multi-lumen catheters; contact pharmacy.

sections.title: IV Complications: Recognition and Response
sections.body:
Phlebitis: redness, warmth, pain along vein. Assess 1–8 scale (Visual Infusion Phlebitis score). Discontinue IV; restart in opposite arm above the problem site.
Infiltration: non-vesicant fluid leaking into tissue. Swelling, coolness, pallor around site. Discontinue; elevate limb; warm compress.
Extravasation: vesicant drug leaking. Same signs but tissue necrosis possible. STOP infusion immediately; leave catheter in temporarily to aspirate; notify physician; apply antidote if available (e.g. hyaluronidase for vinca alkaloids); document site map with photo.
Air embolism: air in IV tubing entering bloodstream. Symptoms: dyspnoea, chest pain, 'millwheel' murmur, altered consciousness. Turn patient left lateral Trendelenburg; call for emergency help; O2 100%; aspiration of air via central catheter if accessible.
Sepsis: fever, chills, rigors during infusion. Remove IV; send tip for culture; blood cultures; notify physician.

content.clinical_pearl: Extravasation of vesicants (especially chemotherapy) is a time-critical emergency. The most critical step is to STOP the infusion immediately while leaving the IV in place so as much drug as possible can be aspirated before removing the catheter. Applying warmth worsens extravasation — cold is typically used for cytotoxics, warm for vinca alkaloids.
key_points: IV gauge selection: larger gauge = faster flow; smaller gauge = less vein trauma
Never co-administer incompatible drugs without flushing
Extravasation of vesicant: stop infusion, leave catheter to aspirate, notify MD immediately
Air embolism: left lateral Trendelenburg position, 100% O2
references: INS Infusion Therapy Standards of Practice 2021

lessons.title: Weight-Based and Paediatric Dose Calculations
lessons.lay_summary: Paediatric medication errors are among the most serious. Weight-based dosing, decimal point errors, and unit confusion are the leading causes.

content.intro: Paediatric dosing is weight-based because children's pharmacokinetics differ fundamentally from adults. Dose errors in children cause disproportionate harm — tenfold dosing errors (decimal point misplacement) are a leading cause of paediatric medication fatalities. Nurses working with children must be proficient in weight-based calculations and understand the concept of ceiling dose.

sections.title: Weight-Based Dosing: mg/kg Calculations
sections.body: Formula: Dose (mg) = Weight (kg) × Dose per kg (mg/kg). Example: paracetamol 15 mg/kg for a 12 kg child = 12 × 15 = 180 mg. Always verify: is the ordered dose within the recommended mg/kg range? Check maximum dose (ceiling). Example: ibuprofen 10 mg/kg in a 30 kg child = 300 mg per dose; adult maximum = 400 mg/dose; 300 mg is acceptable. Critical safety check: never exceed the adult maximum dose in any child, regardless of weight. Document the child's weight used for calculation. Reweigh children at each admission — using estimated or old weights is a frequent error source.

sections.title: Decimal Point and Unit Errors
sections.body: Leading zero rule: ALWAYS write '0.5 mg' never '.5 mg' (a missing decimal point turns 0.5 into 5 — a tenfold error). Trailing zero rule: NEVER write '5.0 mg' — always write '5 mg' (trailing zero can be misread as 50 mg). NEVER abbreviate units in a way that causes ambiguity: write 'units' not 'U' for insulin (U looks like 0 → 10-fold error); write 'micrograms' not 'mcg' or 'μg' in handwriting. High-alert paediatric medications (morphine, potassium, insulin, concentrated solutions): require independent double-check of every calculation. Practical: always calculate and state the formula, the weight used, the calculation, and the final dose before preparing — say it aloud during IDC.

sections.title: Neonatal Calculations and Special Considerations
sections.body: Neonates (0-28 days): immature hepatic and renal function → altered drug metabolism and elimination. Neonatal doses may be expressed per kg, per day, and divided into doses per day — be precise about the meaning. Common neonatal drugs: gentamicin (once daily, extended-interval dosing — check pre-dose trough, target <1 mg/L for standard dosing); caffeine citrate (apnoea of prematurity); surfactant (endotracheal instillation — calculated per kg birthweight). Always confirm: is this a preterm or term neonate? Is gestational age corrected? Are renal and hepatic functions known? Neonatal units have dedicated dosing references (Neofax, BNFc) — never apply adult or standard paediatric references.

content.clinical_pearl: When a calculated paediatric dose looks surprisingly high or low, stop and verify before administering. A useful sanity check: consider the adult dose. If your paediatric dose for a 20 kg child exceeds the adult dose for a drug like paracetamol, you have made an error. Always ask: 'Does this make clinical sense for this size of child?'
key_points: Paediatric dose = Weight (kg) × mg/kg; never exceed adult maximum dose
Leading zero always (0.5 mg), never trailing zero (5 mg, not 5.0 mg)
Write 'units' for insulin, 'micrograms' for mcg — abbreviation errors cause 10-fold overdoses
Neonates: immature metabolism; use NeoFax/BNFc, not adult/standard paediatric references
If the dose looks wrong — STOP, verify before administering
references: ISMP. Medication Safety Alert — paediatric medication errors. 2018
Joint Commission. Preventing paediatric medication errors. Sentinel Event Alert 39, 2008
BNF for Children (BNFc). RCPCH/NPPG/RPSGB. Annual edition

lessons.title: Total Parenteral Nutrition: Nursing Responsibilities
lessons.lay_summary: TPN delivers nutrients directly into the bloodstream. It is life-saving but carries serious risks — infection, metabolic complications, and refeeding syndrome.

content.intro: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) provides all nutritional requirements intravenously when the gastrointestinal tract cannot be used. It is indicated in bowel obstruction, short bowel syndrome, severe malabsorption, prolonged ileus, and high-output intestinal fistulae. TPN requires specialist nutrition team oversight, central venous access, and meticulous nursing monitoring.

sections.title: Central Venous Access and TPN Administration
sections.body: TPN is hypertonic and causes chemical phlebitis in peripheral veins — central venous access is required for long-term TPN (peripheral parenteral nutrition, PPN, with lower osmolarity is used short-term only). Dedicated catheter lumen: TPN should ideally have a dedicated lumen — nothing else administered through the TPN lumen (blood, medications, blood products). Risk of contamination and catheter-associated bloodstream infection (CABSI) with multiple uses. Filter: 0.22 μm in-line filter for standard TPN (removes particulates and air emboli); 1.2 μm filter if lipid-containing admixture. Rate: never change TPN rate abruptly — start at lower rate, titrate up; do not accelerate to 'catch up' missed volume (hyperglycaemia risk).

sections.title: Monitoring and Complications
sections.body: Metabolic monitoring: blood glucose 4-6 hourly initially (hyperglycaemia is the most common complication; target 6-10 mmol/L; insulin sliding scale or infusion often required). Daily: electrolytes, renal function (adjust TPN formulation). Twice weekly: LFTs (TPN-associated liver disease — cholestasis with prolonged use), calcium, magnesium, phosphate, FBC. Refeeding syndrome: occurs in malnourished patients on restarting nutrition (PO or TPN); profound hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia as insulin drives intracellular shift; can cause cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, neurological complications. Prevention: identify at-risk patients (prolonged starvation, low body weight, history of alcohol misuse, minimal intake >5 days); start TPN at no more than 50% target rate × 2 days; supplement electrolytes before and during initiation; thiamine supplementation. Infection: change TPN bag and IV tubing every 24 hours; report fever or rigors in patients on TPN — blood cultures from central line and peripheral site.

content.clinical_pearl: Never run TPN through the same lumen as blood, medications, or blood products — and never piggyback onto the TPN line. The lipid-containing solution in TPN bags (Total Nutrient Admixture, TNA) is an excellent growth medium for micro-organisms. Strict aseptic technique at all connections is not optional — it prevents life-threatening CABSI.
key_points: TPN requires central venous access; peripheral TPN only short-term
Dedicated TPN lumen — nothing else through TPN line
0.22 μm filter (or 1.2 μm if lipid admixture); change bag and line every 24h
Refeeding syndrome: start at ≤50% target rate; supplement phosphate, K+, Mg2+, thiamine
Blood glucose 4-6 hourly; target 6-10 mmol/L; insulin as needed
references: NICE. Guideline NG22: Nutrition support for adults. NICE, 2006 updated 2017
ASPEN. Safe practices for parenteral nutrition. J Parenteral & Enteral Nutrition 2004;28(6):S39-S70
Mehanna HM et al. Refeeding syndrome. BMJ 2008;336:1495-1498

flashcards.question: Basic dose formula for volume to administer?
flashcards.answer: (Dose ordered ÷ Dose on hand) × Vehicle = Volume to give.

flashcards.question: Formula for IV infusion rate in mL/h?
Formula for gravity drip rate (drops/min)?
flashcards.answer: (Volume mL × Drop factor gtt/mL) ÷ (Hours × 60 min) = gtt/min

flashcards.question: First action when vesicant extravasation is suspected?
flashcards.answer: Stop the infusion immediately; leave the catheter in place to aspirate residual drug before removal.

mcq_questions.question: Order: metronidazole 500 mg IV. Available: metronidazole 5 mg/mL in 100 mL NS. How many mL should the nurse administer?
mcq_questions.explanation: 500 mg ÷ 5 mg/mL = 100 mL. The entire 100 mL bag contains exactly 500 mg at 5 mg/mL concentration.

mcq_questions.question: A patient weighing 80 kg is ordered gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV. The available concentration is 40 mg/mL. How many mL should be administered?
mcq_questions.explanation: Step 1: 80 kg × 5 mg/kg = 400 mg. Step 2: 400 mg ÷ 40 mg/mL = 10 mL.

mcq_questions.question: Order: infuse 500 mL of normal saline over 4 hours via gravity drip. Drop factor: 15 gtt/mL. What is the required drip rate in gtt/min? (Round to nearest whole number.)
mcq_questions.explanation: (500 mL × 15 gtt/mL) ÷ (4 h × 60 min) = 7500 ÷ 240 = 31.25 → rounded to 31 gtt/min.

mcq_questions.question: Select ALL signs that indicate IV site phlebitis rather than extravasation.

options.A: Redness and warmth tracking along the vein
options.B: Swelling and coolness around the IV site
options.D: Infusate leaking into subcutaneous tissue visible as puffiness

mcq_questions.explanation: Phlebitis signs: redness + warmth along vein (A), pain along vessel (C), induration/cord-like vein (E). Swelling with coolness (B) and puffiness from fluid leaking into tissue (D) indicate infiltration or extravasation, not phlebitis.

mcq_questions.question: A patient requires an IV infusion of 1000 mL normal saline over 8 hours. The drip factor is 20 drops/mL. What is the correct drip rate in drops per minute?
mcq_questions.explanation: Drip rate = (Volume × drip factor) ÷ time in minutes = (1000 × 20) ÷ 480 = 41.7 ≈ 42 drops/min. Using 125 mL/h confuses flow rate with drip rate. The drip factor must always be incorporated.

mcq_questions.question: A patient weighing 60 kg is ordered dopamine at 5 mcg/kg/min. The available solution is dopamine 400 mg in 250 mL D5W. What is the infusion rate in mL/hour?
mcq_questions.explanation: Step 1: dose = 5 mcg × 60 kg = 300 mcg/min. Step 2: concentration = 400,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 1600 mcg/mL. Step 3: rate = (300 mcg/min) ÷ (1600 mcg/mL) = 0.1875 mL/min × 60 = 11.25 mL/h.

mcq_questions.question: When priming an IV administration set, what is the nurse's main purpose?

options.A: To warm the fluid to body temperature
options.B: To remove air from the tubing before connecting to the patient
options.C: To check the expiry date of the IV bag

mcq_questions.explanation: Priming (purging) the IV set removes air from the tubing to prevent air embolism. Air in peripheral IV lines is rarely fatal at small volumes, but IV air remains dangerous in central lines and in patients with patent foramen ovale. This step is mandatory before connecting to the patient.

mcq_questions.question: A patient has an IV site showing redness, swelling, and warmth along the vein with no fluid leaking. This assessment finding most likely indicates:
mcq_questions.explanation: Phlebitis (inflammation of the vein wall) presents with redness, warmth, pain, and palpable cord along the vein without extravasation. Infiltration shows swelling and coolness from fluid in surrounding tissue. Speed shock causes systemic symptoms. The IV site should be discontinued and documented.

mcq_questions.question: A physician orders heparin 5000 units subcutaneously. The available stock is heparin 10,000 units/mL. How many mL should the nurse administer?
mcq_questions.explanation: 5000 units ÷ 10,000 units/mL = 0.5 mL. Heparin is a high-alert anticoagulant — calculation must be double-checked. A 1 mL subcutaneous dose would deliver double the prescribed dose and risk significant haemorrhage.

mcq_questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer an IV piggyback (IVPB) antibiotic over 30 minutes. The primary line is running at 75 mL/h. When the IVPB bag empties, what should happen?

options.A: The primary IV should be clamped
options.B: The primary IV automatically resumes at its previous rate
options.C: A new IVPB bag should be connected immediately
options.D: The IV line should be flushed and removed

mcq_questions.explanation: After an IVPB empties, backpressure from the primary line (hung lower) resumes flow through the primary tubing at its set rate. This is the design of secondary IV systems — no manual intervention is needed unless using a pump without automatic secondary-to-primary switch.

mcq_questions.question: A patient receiving a blood transfusion suddenly develops fever (38.8°C), chills, and urticaria 20 minutes after the start. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.A: Slow the transfusion rate and observe
options.B: Stop the transfusion, keep the IV line open with normal saline, and notify the physician
options.C: Administer paracetamol and continue the transfusion
options.D: Increase the infusion rate to finish before the reaction worsens

mcq_questions.explanation: Any suspected transfusion reaction (fever, chills, urticaria) requires immediate cessation. The IV line is kept open with NS (not the blood tubing) to maintain access. The physician and blood bank are notified, and the unit is returned. Continuing or slowing the transfusion risks anaphylaxis or acute haemolytic reaction.
